newsitem.title: USA: TWA posts loss, Delta's profits rise, Southwest slips.
newsitem.headline: TWA posts loss, Delta's profits rise, Southwest slips.

text.p: Trans World Airlines Inc. reported a loss Thursday for the latest quarter, due in part to a decline in bookings after the deadly crash of its Flight 800 in July, while Delta Air Lines Inc. reported higher profits.
Southwest Airlines, the budget airline which has grown rapidly over the last five years, saw its earnings slip and announced a major effort to put a lid on creeping costs.
The loss at TWA, however, was much smaller than a year ago, when the carrier was emerging from its second bankruptcy.
St. Louis-based TWA reported a loss of $14.3 million, or 40 cents a share, for the third quarter, compared with a loss of $82 million a year earlier.
Per share figures for the year earlier period were not available. The company emerged from bankrupcty in August, 1995. It had previously been in bankruptcy in 1992-93.
Revenues rose to $1 billion from $959.4 million.

TWA Flight 800 crashed off the coast of Long Island, N.Y., on July 17, killing all 230 aboard. TWA said it suffered a fall-off in advance bookings, an unusually high level of domestic flight cancellations and a loss of premium fare bookings after the crash.

"The events of the summer of 1996 have dealt us a setback," TWA President Jeffrey Erickson said in a statement. "We will redouble our efforts through the remainder of this year and into 1997 to put our rebuilding effort back on track."
The carrier said it believed the drop in bookings was consistent with the experience of other airlines that have suffered similar tragedies.
Erickson said the company was disappointed with its third quarter. The results follow "six consecutive quarters of year-over-year improvement in operating earnings," he said.
TWA stock gained 25 cents to $8.44 on the American Stock Exchange.

Atlanta-based Delta said its earnings rose to $238 million in its first fiscal quarter on revenues of $3.43 billion. A year earlier the international carrier earned $201 million on revenues of $3.19 billion.
Due to a greater number of shares outstanding, per share earnings declined to $3.09 from $3.47 a year earlier.
The airline said the results represented its sixth consecutive quarter of record operating profits.
Delta Chairman Ronald Allen said the earnings were a "direct result" of the company's cost reduction programme.
The airline said passenger traffic grew 12 percent to 25.4 billion revenue passenger miles.
Delta said earnings were affected by a 16 percent year-over-year increase in the price of jet fuel.

"Delta's unit costs during the September 1996 quarter were higher than we expected, largely because of fuel price increases, the Olympics, and costs related to our exceptionally strong traffic," said Allen.
Delta's stock fell 37.5 cents to $69.375 on the New York Stock Exchange.
Dallas-based Southwest Airlines saw its third quarter earnings slip 10 percent from the same period last year.
It said net earnings for the quarter were $60.9 million, or 40 cents a share, down from $67.7 million, or 45 cents per share, a year earlier.
Revenues rose 16.5 percent to $891.5 million but operating costs rose sharply and earnings were hurt by the reimposition of a 10 percent federal ticket tax in August.

"The 21.2 percent increase in average fuel prices and the federal jet fuel tax increased operating expenses by approximately $30 million in third quarter 1996," Chairman Herb Kelleher said in a statement.
Kelleher said October traffic and advanced bookings looked strong but that high fuel prices and the fuel and ticket taxes would also affect fourth quarter earnings.

Chief Financial Officer Gary Kelly announced a package of "very large" cost-reduction initiatives and said the carrier would focus heavily on driving down costs for the next couple of years. Southwest's stock rose 50 cents to $22.125 on the NYSE.
